To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the silencing of the self is a common experience for women with HIV/AIDS and that the transition from silence toward self-advocating action is an individual and contextual process that may be influenced by a variety of factors, including the HIV/AIDS diagnosis, the social context, and the availability of support.
women with HIV reported silencing behaviors that are consistent with feminist literature and that the transition to action may be initiated by a threat to self or by a conscious process of insight.

women living with HIV reported silencing behaviors that are consistent with the literature on women's experiences of silencing, and the silencing experiences may be a protective strategy or a coping mechanism for women living with HIV.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the transition from silence (i.e., self-silencing) to action (i.e., advocacy) and how women with HIV/AIDS make that transition.
the process of women living with AIDS/HIV moving from silencing to action.
the silencing of women's voices and their transition from silence to self-advocating action.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the silencing of women living with AIDS is a process that can be interrupted.
the silencing process is a dynamic process that can be interrupted and changed by a variety of factors.
the transition from silencing the self is a process of self-discovery and empowerment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
women living with HIV and AIDS have a range of experiences that may be described as silencing the self.
women with HIV need to be supported in the transition from silence, to action, to empowerment.
silencing behaviors are a complex and multidimensional phenomenon.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the women who were able to transition to self-advocates were able to do so by learning to value themselves, to trust their own feelings and needs and to express them.
women with HIV are often silenced by the health care system, by the HIV/AIDS community, and by their own internalized beliefs about what it means to be a woman.
women who are diagnosed with HIV/AIDS are often faced with the choice of whether to silence themselves or to speak up for themselves.
